tasks.q: What is the purpose of encryption?
a: To scramble data so only someone with the key can understand it
To stop signals leaving the building
tasks.fb: Encryption doesn't stop interception; it makes intercepted data useless.

tasks.q: Why is encryption especially important for wireless networks?
a: Radio signals can be picked up by anyone within range
tasks.fb: With a cable, an attacker needs physical access. Wireless signals spread out into the air.

a: Anyone who knows the rule can reverse it, because there's no secret key
It can't be decoded at all
tasks.fb: ROT13 is used to hide spoilers or puzzle answers, not to keep secrets.

a: The secret value used to encrypt and decrypt data
The first letter of the message
tasks.fb: Anyone with the key can unlock the message, so the key must be protected.

tasks.q: Why are master keys never sent over the network?
a: They could be intercepted, and then all the data could be decrypted
They are too large to send
tasks.fb: If an attacker captures the key, the encryption is worthless.

tasks.q: Which key can be shared with anyone?
tasks.fb: The public key only locks messages; it can't unlock them.

tasks.q: What happens if someone gets hold of your private key?
a: They can decrypt messages meant only for you
Nothing, as it's useless without the public key
tasks.fb: That's why a private key is never shared.

tasks.q: Put the WPA2 handshake steps in order.
steps: Master key is generated from the wireless password
Random number is sent with the network interface card address
Transient key is calculated from the master key, random numbers and network card addresses
Random number is sent with a message integrity code
Group temporal key is calculated and sent with a message integrity code
Acknowledgement is sent confirming communication can begin
tasks.fb: Both sides calculate the same keys, so the keys themselves never travel over the air.

tasks.q: What does WPA2 do before any data is sent?
a: Checks that both devices know the same key, so they can trust each other

tasks.q: Which network is the safest to use?
a: One protected with WPA2 or WPA3 and a strong password
An open network with no password
One that uses old WEP security
tasks.fb: WEP was cracked years ago, and open networks don't encrypt Wi-Fi traffic.

tasks.q: Why does the strength of the Wi-Fi password matter?
a: The master key is made from it, so a weak password makes the key easier to guess
tasks.fb: Attackers try common passwords to recreate the key.

tasks.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The secret used to encrypt and decrypt
Shared with anyone and used to encrypt
Kept secret and used to decrypt
Scrambling data so it can't be read without the key
tasks.fb: Learn these terms: they come up in exam questions on wireless security.

info.title: Bletchley Park
info.text: In the Second World War, codebreakers at Bletchley Park, including Alan Turing, cracked the German Enigma cipher, which helped shorten the war.

info.title: Caesar's shift
info.text: Julius Caesar is said to have used a shift of 3: A became D, B became E, and so on. That's why shift ciphers are called Caesar ciphers.

info.title: Spoiler alert
info.text: ROT13 is still used online to hide spoilers and puzzle answers: it's easy to reverse, but you won't read it by accident.

info.title: The padlock
info.text: The padlock in your browser means HTTPS, which uses public and private keys to set up a secure connection with the website.

info.title: WEP was cracked
info.text: The first Wi-Fi security, WEP, had serious flaws and could be cracked in minutes. WPA and then WPA2 replaced it.

info.title: WPA3
info.text: WPA3 arrived in 2018. It protects even weak passwords better, by making it much harder to guess them offline.
